smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-01.title: Power of a point
smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-01.body:
The inradius is $2$, so the altitude is $6$ and the side is $4\sqrt3$. Let $F$ be the foot of the altitude on $BC$; it is the midpoint of $BC$ and the point of tangency, so $BF=2\sqrt3$ and $FD$ is a diameter, $FD=4$. Then $BD=\sqrt{BF^2+FD^2}=\sqrt{12+16}=2\sqrt7$. The power of $B$ with respect to the circle is $BF^2=12$ (tangent length squared), so $BE\cdot BD=12$ and $BE=\frac{12}{2\sqrt7}=\frac6{\sqrt7}=\frac{6\sqrt7}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{6\sqrt7}{7}$**

smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-01.title: Coordinates
smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-01.body:
Put $F=(0,0)$, $B=(-2\sqrt3,0)$, center $(0,2)$, $D=(0,4)$. The line $BD$ is $y=\frac{4}{2\sqrt3}(x+2\sqrt3)$. Substituting into $x^2+(y-2)^2=4$ gives the second intersection $E$ at distance $\frac6{\sqrt7}$ from $B$ (the two intersections are at distances $\frac6{\sqrt7}$ and $2\sqrt7$, whose product is $12$).

**Answer: $\frac{6\sqrt7}{7}$**

smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-02.title: Central angles
smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-02.body:
A chord of length $2R\sin\alpha$ subtends the central angle $2\alpha$. Here $R=5$: $AB=6=10\sin\alpha$ gives $\sin\alpha=\frac35,\ \cos\alpha=\frac45$; $AC=8=10\sin\beta$ gives $\sin\beta=\frac45,\ \cos\beta=\frac35$. Depending on whether $B$ and $C$ are on the same side of $A$ or not, the central angle of $BC$ is $2|\beta-\alpha|$ or $2(\alpha+\beta)$ (as $\alpha+\beta=90^\circ$, the latter is a diameter, $BC=10$). The first gives $BC=10\sin(\beta-\alpha)=10\left(\sin\beta\cos\alpha-\cos\beta\sin\alpha\right)=10\cdot\frac{16-9}{25}=\frac{14}5$. The smaller value is $\frac{14}5$.

**Answer: $\frac{14}{5}$**

smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-03.title: Altitude in triangle $ABC$
smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-03.body:
Only triangle $ABC$ matters: $E$ lies on $AC$ with $BA=BE=5$, $EC=7$, $BC=11$. Drop the altitude $BH$ to $AC$; since $BAE$ is isosceles, $H$ is the midpoint of $AE$, so $EH=\frac{AE}2$ and $HC=EH+7$. Then $BH^2=25-EH^2=121-(EH+7)^2$, so $25=72-14EH$ and $EH=\frac{47}{14}$. Hence $AE=2EH=\frac{47}7$.

**Answer: $\frac{47}{7}$**

smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-03.title: Cyclic quadrilateral and Ptolemy
smt-2013-geometry-tiebreaker-03.body:
The isosceles triangles $ABE$ and $DCE$ have equal base angles at $E$ (vertical angles), so $\triangle AEB\sim\triangle DEC$ with $\frac{AE}{DE}=\frac{BE}{CE}=\frac57$. Then $\triangle BEC\sim\triangle AED$ (SAS, vertical angles at $E$), so $\angle EAD=\angle EBC$ and $ABCD$ is cyclic. Let $AE=5x$; then $DE=7x$ and $AD=11x$. Ptolemy: $AB\cdot CD+AD\cdot BC=AC\cdot BD$, i.e. $35+121x=(5x+7)(7x+5)$, so $35x^2=47x$ and $x=\frac{47}{35}$, giving $AE=5x=\frac{47}{7}$.

**Answer: $\frac{47}{7}$**
